title: Reading Hidden Genes From Planned Crosses
endLine: Planned crosses test inheritance rules by comparing offspring counts to probability.

scenes.tts: Where does a vanished trait go when two lines cross? Cross round peas with wrinkled ones, and every hybrid is round. Genes stay hidden, so biologists count offspring from planned crosses.
scenes.caption: Where does a vanished trait go when two lines cross? Cross round peas with wrinkled ones, and every hybrid is round. Genes stay hidden, so biologists count offspring from planned crosses.
scenes.visual: On a dark breeding table that fills the frame, a round pea pod sits top left and a wrinkled pea pod sits top right (schematic). Pollen drifts from one pod to the other; the seed tray below fills with round hybrid seeds, while a ghosted wrinkled seed pulses beside a bold question mark.
scenes.narration: Where does a vanished trait go when two lines cross? Cross round peas with wrinkled ones, and every hybrid is round. Genes stay hidden, so biologists count offspring from planned crosses.

scenes.visual: The pods dim softly while the title 'Reading Hidden Genes From Planned Crosses' appears in large high-contrast type across the center of the breeding table.

scenes.tts: Controlled crosses start with pure lines. Garden pea flowers enclose their reproductive organs inside petals, so they normally self-pollinate. Left alone, a line stays pure. Opened by hand, it can be crossed without stray pollen.
scenes.caption: Controlled crosses start with pure lines. Garden pea flowers enclose their reproductive organs inside petals, so they normally self-pollinate. Left alone, a line stays pure. Opened by hand, it can be crossed without stray pollen.
scenes.visual: At the top of the same breeding table, a closed garden pea flower (Pisum sativum, schematic) sheds pollen onto itself inside its petals, keeping the line pure. Then the petals open as a brush transfers pollen from a wrinkled line to a round line while stray pollen drifts away blocked.
scenes.narration: Controlled crosses start with pure lines. Garden pea flowers enclose their reproductive organs inside petals, so they normally self-pollinate. Left alone, a line stays pure. Opened by hand, it can be crossed without stray pollen.

scenes.tts: Next, let the round hybrids self-pollinate, and count every seed. Gregor Mendel counted seven thousand three hundred twenty-four seeds. Five thousand four hundred seventy-four were round, and one thousand eight hundred fifty were wrinkled. Round divided by wrinkled is two point nine six, nearly three to one.
scenes.caption: Next, let the round hybrids self-pollinate, and count every seed. Gregor Mendel counted 7,324 seeds. 5,474 were round, and 1,850 were wrinkled. Round divided by wrinkled is 2.96, nearly 3:1.
scenes.visual: On the breeding table, the round hybrids self-pollinate and seeds pour into two growing bars computed from Gregor Mendel's counts: 5,474 round and 1,850 wrinkled (7,324 total). As the narrator speaks the math, the formula appears step by step: '5,474 ÷ 1,850 = 2.96', settling beside a '3:1' marker.
scenes.narration: Next, let the round hybrids self-pollinate, and count every seed. Gregor Mendel counted 7,324 seeds. 5,474 were round, and 1,850 were wrinkled. Round divided by wrinkled is 2.96, nearly 3:1.

scenes.tts: Each plant carries two copies of each gene; the versions are called alleles. A hybrid with two different alleles is a heterozygote. Segregation deals one allele per gamete like a fair coin toss. Two heterozygotes fill four equal Punnett square boxes. With complete dominance, one round copy shows: three round to one wrinkled.
scenes.caption: Each plant carries two copies of each gene; the versions are called alleles. A hybrid with two different alleles is a heterozygote. Segregation deals one allele per gamete like a fair coin toss. Two heterozygotes fill four equal Punnett square boxes. With complete dominance, one round copy shows: 3 round to 1 wrinkled.
scenes.visual: Above the center of the breeding table, two heterozygote parents (Aa × Aa, schematic) each split their two allele tokens like flipping coins into eggs and pollen. Those gametes drop into a 2-by-2 Punnett square of four equal boxes (1 AA, 2 Aa, 1 aa); dominance lights the AA and both Aa boxes round, leaving aa wrinkled (3:1).
scenes.narration: Each plant carries two copies of each gene; the versions are called alleles. A hybrid with two different alleles is a heterozygote. Segregation deals one allele per gamete like a fair coin toss. Two heterozygotes fill four equal Punnett square boxes. With complete dominance, one round copy shows: 3 round to 1 wrinkled.

scenes.tts: Planned crosses test inheritance by comparing offspring counts to expected probabilities. Add an unlinked second trait, seed colour, with its own coin. Each hybrid makes four gamete types at one-quarter each, dealing sixteen boxes. Dominance groups them into a nine to three to three to one ratio.
scenes.caption: Planned crosses test inheritance by comparing offspring counts to expected probabilities. Add an unlinked second trait, seed colour, with its own coin. Each hybrid makes four gamete types at 1/4 each, dealing sixteen boxes. Dominance groups them into a 9:3:3:1 ratio.
scenes.visual: The same Punnett square expands smoothly into a 4-by-4 grid (AaBb × AaBb, schematic). Two coins spin per parent, placing AB, Ab, aB, and ab along both edges at 1/4 each to fill sixteen equal boxes. Colour sweeps across the boxes to group them into nine round yellow, three round green, three wrinkled yellow, and one wrinkled green (9:3:3:1).
scenes.narration: Planned crosses test inheritance by comparing offspring counts to expected probabilities. Add an unlinked second trait, seed colour, with its own coin. Each hybrid makes four gamete types at 1/4 each, dealing sixteen boxes. Dominance groups them into a 9:3:3:1 ratio.

scenes.tts: Mendel counted five hundred fifty-six hybrid seeds across those four classes. He got three hundred fifteen, one hundred eight, one hundred one, and thirty-two. Nine sixteenths of five hundred fifty-six predicts three hundred twelve point seven five round yellow. None matched exactly. Does that mismatch break the rule?
scenes.caption: Mendel counted 556 hybrid seeds across those four classes. He got 315, 108, 101, and 32. Nine sixteenths of 556 predicts 312.75 round yellow. None matched exactly. Does that mismatch break the rule?
scenes.visual: Below the sixteen-box grid, four observed bars rise beside four expected bars computed from 9:3:3:1 out of 556 seeds, with '9/16 × 556 = 312.75' written out as it is spoken: 315 vs 312.75 (round yellow), 108 vs 104.25 (round green), 101 vs 104.25 (wrinkled yellow), and 32 vs 34.75 (wrinkled green). Small gap ticks highlight that none matches exactly; the question 'Does that mismatch break the 9:3:3:1 rule?' appears above.
scenes.narration: Mendel counted 556 hybrid seeds across those four classes. He got 315, 108, 101, and 32. Nine sixteenths of 556 predicts 312.75 round yellow. None matched exactly. Does that mismatch break the rule?

scenes.visual: Hold the question 'Does that mismatch break the 9:3:3:1 rule?' on screen over the four paired observed-versus-expected bars (315 vs 312.75, 108 vs 104.25, 101 vs 104.25, 32 vs 34.75) while a subtle timer line glides smoothly across the bottom.

scenes.tts: Not by itself. A cross predicts probabilities, which make a spread of counts, not exact matches. A chi-square score tests whether counts sit inside that usual spread. When a fixed ratio holds, chi-square averages classes minus one, or three here. Higher scores give reason to doubt, never proof.
scenes.caption: Not by itself. A cross predicts probabilities, which make a spread of counts, not exact matches. A chi-square score tests whether counts sit inside that usual spread. When a fixed ratio holds, chi-square averages classes minus one, or 3 here. Higher scores give reason to doubt, never proof.
scenes.visual: Soft shaded spread bands widen around each expected bar (schematic, not computed; no score for Mendel's counts is shown). Beside the chart, a chi-square gauge displays 'classes − 1' turning into '4 − 1 = 3', marked as the average score when the ratio holds, with a caution zone far above labelled 'Reason to doubt'.
scenes.narration: Not by itself. A cross predicts probabilities, which make a spread of counts, not exact matches. A chi-square score tests whether counts sit inside that usual spread. When a fixed ratio holds, chi-square averages classes minus one, or 3 here. Higher scores give reason to doubt, never proof.

scenes.tts: Hidden assumptions can still mislead a cross. Genes close together on one chromosome travel together, breaking independent assortment. Standard ratios also assume equal survival, equal transmission, and accurate scoring. Swapping which parent carries a trait checks whether parental origin matters.
scenes.caption: Hidden assumptions can still mislead a cross. Genes close together on one chromosome travel together, breaking independent assortment. Standard ratios also assume equal survival, equal transmission, and accurate scoring. Swapping which parent carries a trait checks whether parental origin matters.
scenes.visual: On the same breeding table, three quick visual checks transform the grid (schematic): two loci placed close on one chromosome move as a linked pair instead of assorting independently; one Punnett box dims to show unequal survival; then the two parent slots swap sides to test parental origin.
scenes.narration: Hidden assumptions can still mislead a cross. Genes close together on one chromosome travel together, breaking independent assortment. Standard ratios also assume equal survival, equal transmission, and accurate scoring. Swapping which parent carries a trait checks whether parental origin matters.

scenes.tts: Today, Mendel's pea counts are read as segregation and independent assortment. In the first years after, Lucien Cuénot's mouse crosses seemed to break Mendel's rules. They did not. Two yellow alleles kill the embryo, dropping one box, so every live yellow mouse is a heterozygote.
scenes.caption: Today, Mendel's pea counts are read as segregation and independent assortment. In the first years after, Lucien Cuénot's mouse crosses seemed to break Mendel's rules. They did not. Two yellow alleles kill the embryo, dropping one box, so every live yellow mouse is a heterozygote.
scenes.visual: The breeding table shifts from Mendel's pea square (labelled 'Mendel: segregation') to Lucien Cuénot's yellow-mouse 4-box square (schematic): the box with two yellow alleles turns dark and drops out with the label 'dies', leaving only the live heterozygote yellow and non-yellow boxes.
scenes.narration: Today, Mendel's pea counts are read as segregation and independent assortment. In the first years after, Lucien Cuénot's mouse crosses seemed to break Mendel's rules. They did not. Two yellow alleles kill the embryo, dropping one box, so every live yellow mouse is a heterozygote.

scenes.tts: In Morgan's laboratory at Columbia University, a white-eyed Drosophila male was crossed to red-eyed females. Red-eyed offspring of both sexes showed white is recessive. He published the work in Science as sex limited inheritance. Fitting or breaking expectations, counts expose how traits are inherited.

scenes.visual: On the same breeding table, parent slots become Morgan's Drosophila melanogaster cross (schematic): a white-eyed male crossed with red-eyed females produces red-eyed sons and daughters, labelled 'white is recessive'. The table gently zooms back out to frame the Punnett grid and probability gauge together.

scenes.visual: The breeding table fades cleanly to dark slate, leaving only the end-card rule centered in crisp high-contrast type: 'Planned crosses test inheritance rules by comparing offspring counts to probability.'
